transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-27 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Bronze VP Eng), Priya (ML Lead), Carlos (CISO), Ava (Data Scientist), Ellen (Procurement)

Auto-summary (auto): quick intake on per-token unit economics, clarifying deploy options (hosted vs dedicated vs private), and next steps to run unit-econ with customer prompts; security and VPC checklist requested.

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for taking time, quick intro from our side, im Samir Patel, I'm the AE working with fintech and infra teams, with me is Maya Thompson, she's our SE. How's Bronze Capital doing?
[00:14] Jordan: good, thanks. we are exploring adding a question-answer assistant for our trader desk and some doc ingestion for compliance. primary asks are latency under 200ms for short prompts, cost per interaction to fit monthly budget, and strict audit logs.
[00:31] Maya: great, that's the kind of use we see a lot. quick clarifying q, do you expect high token counts per query or mostly short 20-60 token exchanges?
[00:42] Priya: mostly short, maybe 40 tokens on average, but we have long compliance searches that hit 800-1k tokens occasionally. QPS initially low, maybe 10-20 sustained with spikes to 150 during market hours.
[00:58] Samir: perfect. for those profiles we'll look at both batching and prefix caching to control per-token unit cost. quick note on terminology, when I say caching I'm often referring to prefix / KV cache concerns in the runtime.
[01:12] Jordan: quick ask on pricing — what do hosted per-token numbers look like vs dedicated reserved capacity? ballpark is fine.
[01:20] Maya: okay ballpark, for the open-like models we onboarded, hosted per-token list might be around $0.00025 per prompt token and $0.00025 per completion token — roughly $0.0005 per roundtrip depending on lengths. Dedicated reserved capacity tends to be cheaper at scale because you're amortizing GPU costs — could push to an effective per-token of $0.00008 to $0.00015 depending on utilization and batching. those are indicative.
[01:45] Priya: that's a pretty wide band — what's the biggest lever to push it down? is it batching? quantization? model choice?
[01:54] Maya: all of those. big levers: batching (continuous batching on the runtime), prefix/KV caching for repeated context (e.g., system prompts, user history), model selection (smaller distilled models or quantized variants), and reserved capacity. Quantization (4-bit / 8-bit) gives compute savings but can affect quality for some workloads. we typically recommend an eval run with your prompts to see where quality/cost tradeoffs hit.
[02:18] Ava: curious about caching — if we cache participant history for the trader desk, how do you handle cache staleness and privacy? our logs are sensitive.
[02:26] Maya: good question. cache is per-customer and per-model shard; you can set TTLs and also opt out of caching for PII-heavy requests. for Private deployments you can host the KV encrypted in your VPC and control KMS. for hosted we offer customer-scope cache with encryption at rest and access controls. small caveat: some names in the transcription may be off, but configuration is flexible.
[02:49] Carlos: from security standpoint we need KMS integration, bring-your-own-key, and audit logs that are immutable. SOC2 is a given. what does Redwood provide?
[02:58] Samir: we publish SOC2 Type II report, can share the artifact. for Private/VPC we support customer KMS and HSMs for key material; audit logs are available and can be forwarded to your SIEM. we'll include those docs.
[03:14] Ellen: procurement question — what sort of committed spend do you expect for Dedicated? we need a number to start negotiating.
[03:22] Samir: committed capacity depends on model family and throughput; small dedicated pools start at the equivalent of one to two GPUs reserved — in spend terms maybe $Xk/month, but I'll send a concrete pricing sheet after we nail the expected QPS and models.
[03:35] Jordan: can you explain the fallback behavior if the dedicated pool is saturated? we can't have downtimes.
[03:42] Maya: we have smart routing policies — you can tier requests: prefer dedicated, then fallback to hosted compatible variant, the runtime can automatically route and preserve response semantics; you can also set hard fail vs degrade. for critical flows we recommend a canary with a small dedicated pool plus hosted fallback.
[04:02] Priya: about latency — you mentioned 200ms target. what's realistic for 40-token exchanges on hosted vs dedicated?
[04:10] Maya: hosted median for short tokens can be ~60-150ms depending on region and model; dedicated can hit lower tail latency consistently — e.g., 40-80ms if provisioned and not heavily batched. batching increases throughput but can add latency; our continuous batching aims to maximize throughput without blowing p99. we can tune the batch window.
[04:33] Ava: are there any tradeoffs we should expect with aggressive batching for the trader desk (we care about tail latency)?
[04:40] Maya: yes, aggressive batching yields better token economics but raises p95/p99 latency. for low-latency flows we set smaller batch windows or prioritize those requests onto low-latency nodes. you can mix routing policies by endpoint.
[04:55] Jordan: so if we do hosted for non-critical workloads and dedicated for trader desk, that's a common pattern?
[05:01] Samir: exactly. hybrid routing is common — hosted for batch processing and analytics, dedicated for latency sensitive user-facing flows.
[05:09] Carlos: clarify data residency — our compliance requires EU data never leave region. for hosted, can you restrict region?
[05:16] Maya: yes hosted region pinning is supported. private deployments (VPC) are ideal for strict residency / egress controls, and for full control you can run our private on-prem package.
[05:28] Priya: when you quote per-token for dedicated, does that include KV cache savings or is that raw compute?
[05:35] Maya: the dedicated per-token estimate I gave is raw compute amortized; caching and intelligent batching further reduce effective per-token cost. in the cost worksheet we'll show both raw and effective with sample cache-hit rates (e.g., 20-60% cache hit scenarios).
[05:50] Jordan: can you walk us through a quick worked example for our 40-token average and 150 spike pattern?
[05:56] Samir: sure — let me talk through a simple scenario: hosted at $0.0005 per exchange for 40/40 roundtrip that's $0.0005; if you handle 100k exchanges a month that's $50. with spikes you'd pay more during peak. with dedicated and modest batching/caching you might see effective cost drop 3-4x, so that same volume could be $12-15/mo equivalent in compute amortization. exact numbers need the traffic profile.
[06:30] Priya: those $ numbers look optimistic — can we get a spreadsheet?
[06:34] Samir: yes we'll attach a cost model spreadsheet with configurable fields for qps, token lengths, cache hit rate, quantization, and reserved discounts.
[06:40] Ava: what's Redwood's approach to quantization and model variants? we worry about hallucinations on quantized models.
[06:47] Maya: we offer guidance: run your evaluation prompts against quantized variants; for some architectures 4-bit works with negligible quality loss, for others 8-bit is safer. if hallucination is a concern, use a slightly larger model or fall back to higher-precision model for risky queries. we can show delta in evaluation metrics on your prompt set.
[07:04] Jordan: about measurement, do you provide token-level cost telemetry and per-route dashboards?
[07:12] Samir: yep — Redwood Console shows token-level cost, latencies, per-route/model breakdowns, and tracing; you can export to BI.
[07:20] Priya: on the hosted side, what's the SLA?
[07:23] Samir: hosted has best-effort; dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets — specifics depend on enterprise tier. we'll include SLA terms in the package.
[07:32] Carlos: legal question — what about data retention and deletion APIs? we need to ensure we can purge PII.
[07:39] Maya: we have deletion APIs and data retention controls; for Private you can fully control retention locally. for hosted we'll follow standard retention windows and can provide contract language for custom needs.
[07:52] Jordan: can you tell us about onboarding timeline for a pilot? we want to run a 4-week pilot with our prompt set.
[07:58] Maya: typical pilot: week 0-1 onboarding and sample evals, week 2 run unit-econ and perf benchmarks, week 3 iterate on model/config and security checks, week 4 wrap and decision. for private deployments add lead time for network setup and approvals.
[08:16] Ellen: procurement needs estimated cost for pilot to approve spend. give us a ballpark.
[08:20] Samir: pilot pricing varies; often we do a short-term discounted reserved capacity or usage credits. I'll include two options: hosted eval credits vs a 1-month dedicated reserved at a small discount to evaluate.
[08:35] [09:00] -- mid-call technical dive -- Maya starts screen-share (notes truncated in transcript) --
[09:08] Maya: (screen) here's the cost worksheet template — top inputs: avg prompt tokens, avg completion tokens, qps, cache hit rate, batch window, model family, reserved discount. downstream outputs are tokens/month, compute-only cost, effective cost with caching, and implied unit price.
[09:28] Priya: question about batch window — if we set a small window for low latency, how much does that hurt unit cost?
[09:34] Maya: depends on traffic shape; with spiky QPS you lose batching efficiency. in steady state 20-50ms batch windows can reduce cost a lot. if you have long idle times the benefit is lower. we show sensitivity analysis in the sheet.
[09:50] Jordan: are streaming responses billed differently? we plan to stream partial results for long docs.
[09:56] Maya: streamed tokens are billed similarly per-token; but streaming keeps latency down for the front tokens but may incur more compute depending on model behavior.
[10:04] Ava: oh and on the KV cache: do you dedupe frequently used prompt fragments? our users often reuse policy snippets.
[10:12] Maya: yes the caching includes prefix dedupe; you can precompute embeddings for certain repeated contexts or stash canonical system prompts. that substantially raises effective cache hits.
[10:23] Carlos: for private, what's the network topology requirement — do you need full egress or can you allow no public egress?
[10:30] Maya: private on-prem can be fully air-gapped; VPC option talks to a control plane but supports private link and restricted egress. we'll send the VPC checklist.
[10:44] Priya: any pitfalls folks often hit on unit-econ modeling?
[10:48] Maya: common mistakes: underestimating cache hit rates, ignoring tail latency cost of batching, not accounting for tooling/observability cost, and failing to model retries/backoff on spikes. also model selection matters — switching to slightly smaller model can be 2-3x cheaper but needs eval for quality.
[11:10] Jordan: let's capture deliverables before we close.
[11:14] Samir: recap: we'll send cost worksheet + pricing scenarios, SOC2 + KMS/HSM notes, VPC checklist; Maya will schedule a technical deep dive for private deployment; Priya will provide sample prompts and traffic distribution.
[11:28] Priya: timeline looks good. Carlos: i'll review security docs and come with a prioritized questions list.
[11:35] Ellen: procurement will review pilot pricing once we get the worksheet.
[11:40] Samir: cool. anything else?
[11:42] Jordan: one more quick thing — do you support role-based quotas so we can stage internal vs trader desk access?
[11:49] Maya: yes RBAC and per-token quotas per api key/route are supported. we'll include sample configs.
[11:57] Samir: thanks all, we'll follow up with the packet and calendar invite for deep dive.
[12:03] [call ends]
